71. Avoid "Good Ideas"

作者：Greg Nyberg

Good ideas kill projects. Sometimes it’s a quick death, but often it’s a slow, lingering death caused by missed milestones and a spiraling bug count.

好主意杀项目。有时是快死，但经常是缓慢、缠绵的死——由错过里程碑和螺旋上升的 bug 数造成。

You know the kinds of good ideas I’m talking about: tempting, no-brainer, innocent-looking, couldn’t-possibly-hurt-to-try sorts of ideas. They usually occur to someone on the team about halfway through a project when everything seems to be going fine. Stories and tasks are getting knocked off at a good pace, initial testing is going well, and the rollout date looks solid. Life is good.

你知道我说的是哪种好主意：诱人的、想当然的、看起来无辜的、试试也不会有什么坏处的那种。它们通常在项目中途、一切看似顺利时被团队某个人想到。故事和任务以不错的速度被干掉，初测顺利，发布日期看起来稳。生活美好。

Someone has a “good idea,” you acquiesce, and suddenly you are refitting a new version of Hibernate into your project to take advantage of the latest features, or implementing AJAX in some of your web pages because the developer showed the user how cool it is, or even revisiting the database design to utilize XML features of the RDBMS. You tell the project manager you need a few weeks to implement this “good idea,” but it ends up impacting more code than originally anticipated, and your schedule starts to slip. Plus, by letting in the first “good idea,” you’ve allowed the proverbial camel’s nose in the tent, and soon the good ideas are coming out of the woodwork and it becomes harder to say no (and the camel is soon sleeping in your bed).

有人有个「好主意」，你同意了，突然你在项目里重新适配新版本 Hibernate 利用最新特性，或因为开发给用户展示有多酷就在某些网页实现 AJAX，甚至重新审视数据库设计以利用 RDBMS 的 XML 特性。你告诉项目经理需要几周实现这个「好主意」，结果它影响的代码比预期多，进度开始滑。加上，让第一个「好主意」进来，你已经让骆驼鼻子进了帐篷，很快好主意从各个角落冒出来，说不就更难了（骆驼很快睡你床上了）。

The really insidious thing about “good ideas” is that they are “good.” Everyone can recognize and reject “bad” ideas out of hand—it’s the good ones that slip through and cause trouble with scope, complexity, and sheer wasted effort incorporating something into the application that isn’t necessary to meet the business need.

「好主意」真正阴险的地方在于它们是「好」的。每个人都能认出并立刻拒绝「坏」主意——正是好主意溜进来，在范围、复杂度和把不必要的东西塞进应用的纯粹浪费上制造麻烦。

Here are some key phrases to look for:

下面是一些要找的关键词：

“Wouldn’t it be cool if….” Really, any sentence with the word “cool” in it • is a danger signal.

「如果……不是很酷吗？」真的，任何带「酷」字的句子都是危险信号。

“Hey, they just released version XXX of the YYY framework. We ought to • upgrade!”

「嘿，他们刚发布了 YYY 框架的 XXX 版。我们该升级！」

“You know, we really should refactor XXX as long as we are working on • ZZZ….”

「你知道，我们在做 ZZZ 时真该顺便重构 XXX……」

“That XXX technology is really powerful! Maybe we could use it on….” •

「那个 XXX 技术真强大！也许我们可以用在……」

“Hey, < • yournamehere >, I’ve been thinking about the design and I have an idea!”

「嘿，<你的名字>，我一直在想设计，我有个主意！」

OK, OK, maybe I’m being a bit too cynical with that last one. But keep watching out for “good ideas” that can kill your project.

好吧，最后那个可能我有点太愤世嫉俗。但继续提防能杀项目的「好主意」。

72. Great Content Creates Great Systems

作者：Zubin Wadia

I have seen my fair share of initiatives focus endlessly on requirements, design, development, security, and maintenance, but not on the actual point of the system—the data. This is especially true in content-based systems in which the data is information delivered as unstructured or semi-structured content. Great content means the difference between a system that is hollow and one that is relevant.

我见过不少项目无休止地聚焦需求、设计、开发、安全和维护，但不聚焦系统的真正目的——数据。在基于内容的系统里尤其如此，其中数据是以非结构化或半结构化内容交付的信息。伟大内容意味着空洞系统和相关系统之间的区别。

Content is king. Content is the network. Content is the interface. In an increasingly interconnected world, content quality is rapidly becoming the difference between success and failure. FaceBook versus Orkut/Google versus Cuil/ NetFlix versus BlockbusterOnline…the list is endless where battles have been won and lost on the content battlefield. One could argue that content-related aspects are not the software architect’s problem—but I think the next decade will certainly disprove that.

内容为王。内容就是网络。内容就是接口。在日益互联的世界里，内容质量正迅速成为成败的区别。Facebook vs Orkut/Google vs Cuil/Netflix vs BlockbusterOnline……在内容战场上输赢的例子没完没了。有人会说内容相关方面不是软件架构师的问题——但我认为下一个十年肯定会反驳这个。

Part of the design process for a new system should be devoted to assessing content inventory. Designing an effective domain/object/data model is not enough.

新系统设计过程的一部分应该用于评估内容库存。设计有效的领域/对象/数据模型不够。

Analyze all available content and assess its value on the following criteria:

分析所有可用内容，按以下标准评估价值：

Is there enough content available? If not, how do we attain critical mass? •

内容够吗？不够的话，我们怎么达到临界质量？

Is the content fresh enough? If not, how do we improve delivery rates? •

内容够新鲜吗？不够的话，我们怎么提高交付率？

Have all possible content channels been explored? RSS feeds, email, and • paper forms are all channels.

所有可能的内容渠道都探索了吗？RSS 源、邮件、纸质表格都是渠道。

Are there effective input streams built to facilitate the continual delivery • of this content into the system? It’s one thing to identify valuable content, but another thing altogether to harvest it regularly.

有没有建有效的输入流来持续把内容交付进系统？识别有价值内容是一回事，定期收获是另一回事。

Make no mistake, the success of a system depends on its content. Spend a healthy part of the design process to assess the value of your content. If your findings are less than satisfactory, then that’s a red flag the stakeholders must be advised about. I have seen many systems that fulfill all contractual obligations, meet every requirement, and still fail because this fairly obvious aspect was ignored. Great content creates great systems.

别搞错，系统的成功取决于它的内容。花设计过程健康的一部分评估你内容的价值。如果发现不那么满意，那就是要告知干系人的红旗。我见过很多系统履行了所有合同义务、满足每个需求，但仍然失败，因为这个相当明显的方面被忽略了。伟大内容创造伟大系统。

Zubin Wadia Zubin Wadia is CEO at RedRock IT Solutions and CTO at ImageWork Technologies. He has a diverse software programming background with knowledge of Basic, C, C++, Perl, Java, JSP, JSF, JavaScript, Erlang, Scala, Eiffel, and Ruby languages. His main focus is on enabling Fortune Global 500 companies and U.S. government agencies through business process-automation solutions.

Zubin Wadia Zubin Wadia 是 RedRock IT Solutions 的 CEO 和 ImageWork Technologies 的 CTO。他有多样的软件编程背景，懂 Basic、C、C++、Perl、Java、JSP、JSF、JavaScript、Erlang、Scala、Eiffel 和 Ruby。他主要通过业务流程自动化方案服务财富全球 500 强和美国政府机构。

73. The Business Versus the Angry Architect

作者：Chad LaVigne

There comes a time in our careers as architects when we realize many of the issues we encounter are recurring. Though the project and industry may change, many of the problems are similar. At this point we can draw on our experience to provide many solutions quickly, leaving more time to enjoy the challenging issues. We’re confident in our solutions and we deliver as advertised. We have reached homeostasis. This is the perfect time to make a colossal mistake—like deciding you know so much that it’s time for you to start talking more than you listen. This poor decision usually comes with a side of cynicism, impatience, and general anger toward inferior minds who dare contradict your superior understanding of all things technical and otherwise.

在我们架构师生涯中，总有一天意识到遇到的很多问题是反复出现的。虽然项目和行业可能变，很多问题类似。这时我们可以利用经验快速提供很多方案，留更多时间享受有挑战的问题。我们对方案有信心，按广告交付。我们达到了稳态。这是犯大错的完美时机——比如觉得你懂得够多了，该开始说比听多了。这个差决定通常带着愤世嫉俗、不耐烦、以及对比你技术和其他方面高超理解还敢反驳的低等头脑的普遍愤怒。

In its worst form this overconfidence bleeds into the business realm. This is an excellent way to land your career on a list somewhere next to the Black Rhino. The business is our reason for existence. That statement probably hurts a little, but we must not lose sight of that fact. We live to serve them, not vice versa. Listening to and understanding the business that employs us to solve problems is the most critical skill we possess. Ever caught yourself impatiently waiting for a business analyst to finish talking so you could make your point? Chances are, you didn’t get his. Show the business domain experts the respect you expect to receive; this is the last group of people you want viewing you as unapproachable. If they start avoiding you, you’re being a catalyst for communication breakdown and sabotaging your own project. Remember, when you’re talking you can only hear something you already know. Don’t ever start thinking you’re so smart that no one else has something valuable to say.

最糟形式下这种过度自信渗到业务领域。这是把你职业放到黑犀牛旁边某个列表上的好方法。业务是我们存在的理由。这句话可能有点痛，但我们不能忽视这个事实。我们活着是为了服务他们，不是反过来。倾听和理解雇我们解决问题的业务，是我们拥有的最关键技能。有没有过你不耐烦地等业务分析师说完好让你表达观点？很可能你没听懂他的。给业务领域专家你希望得到的尊重；这是你最不想看作难以接近的一群人。如果他们开始躲你，你就是沟通破裂的催化剂、在 sabotage 自己的项目。记住，当你说话时你只能听到你已经知道的东西。别开始觉得自己聪明到别人没什么有价值的可说。

When we are listening, we’ll often disagree with what we hear about how the business operates. That’s fine. We can make suggestions for improvement and should definitely do so. However, if at the end of the day you disagree with how the business is run and it’s not going to change, that’s just too bad. Don’t allow yourself to become a disgruntled genius who spends all of his time trying to impress others by making witty, condescending statements about how poorly the company is run. They won’t be impressed. They’ve met that guy before and they don’t really like him. One of the key ingredients to the recipe for a great architect is passion for your work, but you don’t want too much passion of the angry variety. Learn to accept disagreements and move on. If the differences are too great and you find yourself continually at odds with the business, find a company that’s easier for you to get behind and design solutions for them. Regardless of how, find a way to establish a good relationship with the business and don’t let your ego damage it. It will make you a happier, more productive architect.

当我们倾听时，我们经常不同意听到的业务运作方式。那没问题。我们可以提改进建议，也应该这么做。然而，如果一天结束时你不同意业务运作方式而它不会改变，那也太糟了。别让自己变成不满的天才，把所有时间花在通过关于公司运营多差的机智、居高临下的言论来 impress 别人。他们不会被 impress。他们见过那家伙，不太喜欢他。伟大架构师配方里的关键成分之一是对工作的热情，但你不想要太多愤怒品种的热情。学会接受分歧继续走。如果分歧太大、你发现自己持续和业务不合，找一家你更容易支持、为之设计方案的公司。不管怎样，找办法和业务建立好关系，别让你的自我破坏它。这会让你成为更快乐、更高产的架构师。

74. Stretch Key Dimensions to See What Breaks

作者：Stephen Jones

An application’s design is outlined  initially based on the specified business requirements, selected or existing technologies, performance envelope, expected data volumes, and the financial resources available to build, deploy, and operate it. The solution, whatever it is, will meet or exceed what is asked of it in the contemporary environment and is expected to run successfully (or it is not yet a solution).

应用设计最初基于指定业务需求、选的或现有技术、性能范围、预期数据量、以及构建部署运营的财务资源勾勒。方案不管是什么，会满足或超过当代环境下对它的要求，并预期成功运行（否则还不是方案）。

Now take this solution and stretch the key dimensions to see what breaks.

现在拿这个方案拉关键维度看什么会断。

This examination looks for limits in the design that will occur when, for example, the system becomes wildly popular and more customers use it, the products being processed increase their transaction counts per day, or six months of data must now be retained rather than the initially specified week. Dimensions are stretched individually and then in combination to tease out the unseen limits that might lie hidden in the initial design.

这个检查找设计里的极限，比如系统突然爆火、更多客户用、被处理产品每天交易数增加、或现在要保留六个月数据而不是最初指定的一周。维度单独拉，然后组合拉，挑出可能藏在初始设计里的看不见的极限。

Stretching key dimensions allows an architect to validate a solution by:

拉关键维度让架构师通过以下方式验证方案：

Understanding whether the planned infrastructure accommodates these • increases, and where the limits are. If the infrastructure will break, this process identifies where it will break, which can be highlighted for the application’s owner, or the planned infrastructure can be purchased with specific upgrade paths in mind.

理解计划的基础设施能否容纳这些增长、极限在哪。如果基础设施会断，这个过程识别在哪断，可以突出给应用所有者，或者买计划基础设施时心里有具体升级路径。

Confirming that there are sufficient hours in the day to perform the pro- • cessing at the expected throughput, with head room to accommodate “busy days” or “catch up” after an outage. A solution that cannot complete a day’s processing in a day and relies on the weekend when things are quieter has no long-term future.

确认一天有足够小时在预期吞吐下做处理，有余量容纳「忙日」或 outage 后「追赶」。一个一天完不成一天处理、靠周末闲时的方案没有长期未来。

Validating that the data access choices that were made are still valid as the • system scales. What might work for a week’s worth of data may be unusable with six month’s data loaded.

验证做的数据访问选择在系统扩展时仍有效。对一周数据有效的可能在六个月数据加载后不能用。

Confirming how the application’s increased workload will be scaled • across additional hardware (if required), and the transition path as the load increases. Working through the transition before the application is deployed can influence the data stored and its structure.

确认应用增加的工作负载怎么在额外硬件上扩展（如果需要），以及负载增加时的过渡路径。在应用部署前走完过渡可以影响存储的数据及其结构。

Confirming that the application can still be recovered if the data vol- • umes are increased and/or the data is now split among an increased infrastructure.

确认数据量增加和/或数据现在分散到更多基础设施上时应用仍能恢复。

Based on this examination, elements of the design may be recognised as problems requiring redesign. The redesign will be cheaper whilst the design is still virtual, technical choices are not locked-in and the business data has yet to be stored in the repositories.

基于这个检查，设计的元素可能被识别为需要重设计的问题。在设计还是虚拟、技术选择没锁定、业务数据还没存进仓库时重设计更便宜。

Stephen Jones Stephen Jones designs solutions for Tier-1 Telco Billing and its related high-volume processes for companies such as Telstra and Optus in Australia, and the 1997 version of AT&T in the U.S. This design work included the initial implementations of Telco billing systems, redesigns of post-bill dispute and fraud billing functions, and over two years managing 24/7 production support for Telstra.

Stephen Jones Stephen Jones 为澳大利亚 Telstra、Optus 和美国 1997 版 AT&T 等公司设计一线电信计费及相关高吞吐流程方案。设计工作包括电信计费系统初始实现、账后争议和欺诈计费功能重设计，以及两年多管理 Telstra 24/7 生产支持。

75. If You Design It, You Should Be Able to Code It

作者：Mike Brown

In architecture,  it’s tempting to create elaborate designs and abstractions that elegantly address the problem at hand. It is even more tempting to sprinkle new technologies into the project. At the end of the day, someone has to implement your design, and the architectural acrobatics that you have the developers perform impact the project.

在架构中，很容易创建精心设计、优雅解决眼前问题的设计和抽象。在项目里撒新技术甚至更诱人。一天结束时，有人得实现你的设计，你让开发做的架构杂技影响项目。

When designing the architecture for your project, you need to have a feel for the amount of effort necessary to implement each element of your design; if you’ve developed an element before, it will be much easier to estimate the effort required.

设计项目架构时，你需要对实现设计每个元素所需工作量有感觉；如果你之前开发过一个元素，估算所需努力容易得多。

Don’t use a pattern in your design that you haven’t personally implemented before. Don’t rely on a framework that you haven’t coded against before. Don’t use a server that you haven’t configured before. If your architecture depends on design elements that you haven’t personally used, there are a number of negative side effects:

不要在设计里用你没亲自实现过的模式。不要依赖你没写过代码的框架。不要用你没配置过的服务器。如果架构依赖你没用过的设计元素，有几个负面副作用：

You will not have experienced the learning curve that your developers will • have to face. If you don’t know how long it takes to learn a new technology, you won’t be able to give a good estimate on time to implement.

你不会经历开发要面对的学习曲线。不知道学新技术要多久，就不能给实现时间好估算。

You will not know the pitfalls to avoid when using the elements. Inevita- • bly, things will not go as well as the demo that the trained expert in the technology provided. If you haven’t worked with the technology before, you will be blindsided when this happens.

你不知道用这些元素要避免的坑。不可避免，事情不会像技术训练有素专家的 demo 那么顺。如果你之前没用过这技术，发生时会被 blindsided。

You will lose the confidence of your developers. When they ask questions • about the design and you aren’t able to give solid answers, they will quickly lose confidence in you and your design.

你会失去开发的信任。他们问设计问题你给不出扎实答案时，他们很快对你和你的设计失去信心。

You will introduce unnecessary risk. Not knowing these things can put a • big question mark on key elements of the solution. No one wants to start a project with big, unnecessary risks hanging around.

你会引入不必要风险。不知道这些会给方案关键元素打大问号。没人想在项目开始时挂着大的不必要风险。

So how does one go about learning new frameworks, patterns, and server platforms? Well, that’s another axiom in and of itself: before anything, an architect is a developer.

那怎么学新框架、模式和服务器平台呢？那本身是另一条公理：在任何事之前，架构师是开发。

76. A Rose by Any Other Name Will End Up As a Cabbage

作者：Sam Gardiner

I overheard some people deciding  that they need more layers in their architecture. They were right, as it happens, but going about it a little backward. They were attempting to create a framework that would contain the business logic. Rather than solving some specific problems they started with the idea that they want a framework that wraps the database up and produces objects. And it should use object-relational mapping. And messages. And web services. And it should do all sorts of cool stuff.

我偶然听到一些人决定他们架构需要更多层。他们其实是对的，但做法有点倒过来。他们试图创建一个包含业务逻辑的框架。不是解决某些具体问题，而是从想要一个包装数据库、产出对象的框架这个想法开始。它该用对象关系映射。还有消息。还有 Web 服务。它该做各种酷东西。

Unfortunately, since they didn’t exactly know what cool stuff it would do, they didn’t know what to call it. So they held a little competition to suggest a name. And that is the point at which you must recognise that you have a problem: if you don’t know what a thing should be called, you cannot know what it is. If you don’t know what it is, you cannot sit down and write the code.

不幸的是，因为他们并不确切知道它会做什么酷东西，不知道叫它什么。于是他们办了个小竞赛起名。这就是你必须认识到有问题的点：如果你不知道一个东西该叫什么，你就不能知道它是什么。如果你不知道它是什么，你就不能坐下写代码。

In this particular case, a quick browse throughout the source control history revealed the depth of the problem. Of course, there were lots of empty interface “implementations”! And the really funny thing is that they had already changed the names three times with no actual code. When they started they called it ClientAPI—the “client” refers to the customers of the business, not client as in “client-server”—and the final version was called ClientBusinessObjects. Great name: vague, broad, and misleading.

这个具体案例里，快速翻源码控制历史揭示了问题深度。当然，有很多空接口「实现」！最好笑的是他们已经改了三次名却没有实际代码。开始时叫 ClientAPI——「client」指业务的客户，不是客户端-服务器的 client——最终版叫 ClientBusinessObjects。好名字：模糊、宽泛、误导。

Of course, in the end, a name is just a pointer. Once everyone involved knows that the name is just a name and not a design metaphor then you can all move on. However, if you can’t agree on a name that is specific enough for you to know when it is wrong, then you might have some difficulty even getting started. Design is all about trying to fulfill intentions—e.g., fast, cheap, flexible—and names convey intentions.

当然，最终名字只是指针。一旦所有人都知道名字只是名字不是设计隐喻，你们都可以继续。然而，如果你不能就一个具体到你能知道什么时候它错了的名字达成一致，你可能连开始都困难。设计就是试图实现意图——比如快、便宜、灵活——名字传达意图。

If you can’t name it, you can’t write it. If you change the name three times, then you should stop until you know what you are trying to build.

如果你不能命名它，你就不能写它。如果你改了三次名，那你该停下来，直到知道你要建什么。

After a lifetime of playing with computers—starting with writing games in BASIC on the BBC computer and going on to such diverse elements as pascal, Mathematica, and using Labview to process hand-rolled databases made of raw text data files from experiments held together with sticky tape—Sam Gardiner stumbled into professional software development. He has been working in the software industry for six years.

玩了一辈子计算机——从 BBC 电脑上用 BASIC 写游戏，到 Pascal、Mathematica、Labview 处理用实验原始文本数据文件加胶带凑成的手搓数据库——Sam Gardiner 磕磕绊绊进入专业软件开发。他在软件业工作六年了。

77. Stable Problems Get High-Quality Solutions

作者：Sam Gardiner

Real-world programming is not about solving the problem that someone gives to you. In the computer science classroom, you must solve the binarysort problem given to you. In the real world, the best architects don’t solve hard problems, they work around them. The skill is in drawing boundaries around diffuse and diverse software problems so that they are stable and selfcontained.

现实世界编程不是解决别人给你的问题。在计算机科学课堂上，你必须解决给你的二分排序问题。在现实世界，最好的架构师不解决难题，他们绕着走。技能在于给发散多样的软件问题画边界，让它们稳定、自包含。

An architect should be able to look at a whole mess of concepts and data and process and separate them into smaller pieces or “chunks.” The important thing about those problem chunks is that they are stable, allowing them to be solved by a system chunk that is finite and stable in scope. The problem chunks should be:

架构师应该能面对一大堆概念、数据和过程，把它们分成更小块或「chunks」。这些问题块的重要之处是它们稳定，让有限、范围稳定的系统块能解决它们。问题块应该：

Internally cohesive: the chunk is conceptually unified, so all of the tasks, • data, and features are related

内聚：块在概念上统一，所有任务、数据和功能相关

Well separated from other chunks: the chunks are conceptually normal- • ized; there is little or no overlap between them

和其他块良好分离：块在概念上规范化，它们之间很少或没有重叠

The person who is excessively good at doing this may not even know that she is doing it, just as a person with a good sense of direction knows where she is. It just seems to make sense to her to break up the tasks, data, and features in a way that provides a nice edge or interface to the system. I’m not talking about the actual interfaces of an object-oriented language, but system boundaries.

过分擅长这个的人可能自己都不知道在做，就像方向感好的人知道自己在哪。以给系统提供好边界或接口的方式拆分任务、数据和功能，对她来说就是顺理成章。我说的不是面向对象语言的实际接口，而是系统边界。

For instance, a relational database management system has a very nice system boundary. It manages literally any type of data that can be serialized into a stream of bytes, and it can organize, search, and retrieve that data. Simple.

比如，关系数据库管理系统有非常好的系统边界。它管理字面上任何能序列化成字节流的数据，能组织、搜索、检索那些数据。简单。

What is interesting is that if the problem is stable, then when it is solved, it is solved permanently. In five/fifty years’ time you might want to slap a web/ telepathic interface over it, but your core system won’t need to change. The system is durable because the problem is durable.

有趣的是，如果问题稳定，解决了就永久解决了。五/五十年后你可能想在它上面加个 Web/心灵感应接口，但核心系统不需要变。系统持久因为问题持久。

Of course, the code needs to be pretty neat, but if the problem is neat, the code can be neat, as there are no special cases. And neat code is good because it is easy to test and easy to review, and that means that the implementation quality can be very high. As you don’t have messy code, you can concentrate on things that are outside the domain of user-visible features like using reliable messaging or distributed transactions, or driving up performance by using multithreading or even low-level languages like assembly code. Because the problem isn’t changing, you can concentrate on driving up the quality to the point where it is a feature.

当然代码需要相当整洁，但如果问题整洁，代码就能整洁，因为没有特殊情况。整洁代码好因为它容易测试和审查，意味着实现质量可以非常高。因为你没有乱代码，你可以专注用户可见功能之外的事——比如用可靠消息或分布式事务，或用多线程甚至汇编这样的低级语言提升性能。因为问题不变，你可以专注把质量提升到它成为一个特性的程度。

A stable problem allows you to create a system with a stable design; stable design allows you to concentrate on making an application that has very high quality.

稳定问题让你创建设计稳定的系统；稳定设计让你专注做高质量的应用。

78. It Takes Diligence

作者：Brian Hart

An architect’s job is often portrayed as an activity focused on ingenuity and problem solving. Ingenuity is a key trait of successful architects. However, an equally important characteristic of the activities of a successful architect is diligence. Diligence can manifest itself in many ways, but ultimately it is an exercise in perseverance and paying the right amount of attention to each task and each architectural goal of the system.

架构师的工作经常被描绘成聚焦聪明才智和问题解决的活动。聪明是成功架构师的关键特质。然而，成功架构师活动同等重要的特点是勤奋。勤奋可以多种方式表现，但最终它是毅力的练习，以及对每个任务和系统每个架构目标给以恰当程度的关注。

Diligence goes hand in hand with the mundane. Successful architecture practices are in many ways mundane. Effective architects often follow mundane daily and weekly checklists to remind them of that which they already know academically, but fail to practice by habit. Without such mundane checklists and reminders, architects can quickly fall into software time, in which no measurable progress is achieved because a lack of diligence allowed the architecture to meander and violate known academic principles. It is important to realize in these retrospectives of failed projects that in most cases it isn’t incompetence that drove failure, but rather the lack of both diligence and a sense of urgency.

勤奋和平凡手拉手。成功的架构实践在很多方面是平凡的。高效架构师经常遵循平凡的日/周检查清单，提醒他们那些学术上知道但没习惯实践的事。没有这种平凡检查清单和提醒，架构师会很快掉进软件时间——没有可衡量进展，因为缺乏勤奋让架构漫游、违反已知学术原则。在失败项目的回顾中重要的是认识到：大多数情况下不是无能导致失败，而是缺乏勤奋和紧迫感。

Diligence also requires an architect to succeed at the deceptively simple task of making and keeping commitments. These commitments are often disparate and can encompass a wide range of constraints and expectations. Examples include:

勤奋还要求架构师成功完成看似简单的承诺和信守承诺任务。这些承诺经常是各异的，涵盖广泛约束和期望。例子包括：

Embracing the budget and time constraints of the customer •

拥抱客户的预算和时间约束

Performing all the work that makes the architect effective, not just the • work the architect enjoys

做所有让架构师有效的工作，不只是架构师喜欢的工作

Committing to the process/methodology •

对过程/方法论承诺

Accepting responsibility •

接受责任

Atul Gawande, in his terrific book Better: A Surgeon’s Notes on Performance (Metropolitan Books), speaks of diligence in the medical community:

Atul Gawande 在他的好书《Better: A Surgeon's Notes on Performance》（Metropolitan Books）里谈到医学界的勤奋：

True success in medicine is not easy. It requires will, attention to detail, and creativity. But the lesson I took from India was that it is possible anywhere and by anyone. I can imagine few places with more difficult conditions. Yet astonishing success could be found… what I saw was: Better is possible. It does not take genius. It takes diligence. It takes moral clarity. It takes ingenuity. And above all, it takes a willingness to try.

医学上真正的成功不容易。它需要意志、对细节的关注和创造力。但我从印度学到的教训是：任何地方、任何人都可能做到。我想不出条件更困难的地方。然而惊人的成功能找到……我看到的是：更好是可能的。不需要天才。需要勤奋。需要道德清明。需要聪明。最重要的是，需要愿意尝试。

Brian Hart Brian Hart is an executive consultant with CGI, a leading IT and business process services provider. Brian is involved in the architecture and design of J2EE applications primarily in the state and local government sector. He has been involved in the software industry since 1997.

Brian Hart Brian Hart 是 CGI（领先 IT 和业务流程服务提供商）的执行顾问。Brian 主要在州和地方政府部门参与 J2EE 应用架构和设计。他从 1997 年起在软件业。

79. Take Responsibility for Your Decisions

作者：Yi Zhou

Software architects have to take responsibility for their decisions, as they have much more influential power in software projects than most people in organizations. Studies of software projects show that more than two-thirds of them either are outright failures or deliver unsuccessfully (deadline slip, budget overruns, or low customer satisfaction). Many of the root causes point to improper decisions software architects made, or failures of follow-through on the right architectural decisions.

软件架构师必须为自己的决定负责，因为他们在软件项目里比组织里大多数人有更大影响力。软件项目研究显示三分之二以上要么 outright 失败、要么不成功交付（延期、超预算、客户满意度低）。很多根本原因指向软件架构师做的不当决定，或对正确架构决定的跟进失败。

How can you become a responsible software architect who makes effective architectural decisions?

你怎么成为一个做有效架构决定的负责任软件架构师？

First, you have to be fully cognizant of your decision process, whether it is agile or ceremonial. You should not claim that an architectural decision has been made until the following two conditions are met:

首先，你必须完全清楚自己的决策过程，不管它是敏捷的还是仪式化的。在以下两个条件满足前，你不应声称做了架构决定：

A decision has been put in writing because architectural decisions are • rarely trivial. They must be substantiated and traceable.

决定已经书面记录，因为架构决定很少琐碎。它们必须被证实和可追溯。

A decision has been communicated to the people who execute it and the • people who will be affected directly or indirectly. Communication is all about creating shared understanding.

决定已经沟通给执行它的人、以及直接或间接受影响的人。沟通就是创造共同理解。

Second, review your architectural decisions periodically. Examine the results of your decisions against expectations. Identify architectural decisions that remain valid and those that do not.

第二，定期审查你的架构决定。对照期望检查决定的结果。识别仍有效的架构决定和不再有效的。

Third, enforce your architectural decisions. Many software projects get software architects involved only in the design phase, then they move on to other projects or the consultation contract ends. How can they ensure that their deliberate architectural decisions have been implemented correctly? Their decisions will be at best good intentions unless they follow through with them.

第三，强制执行你的架构决定。很多软件项目只在设计阶段让软件架构师介入，然后他们去其他项目或咨询合同结束。他们怎么确保自己深思熟虑的架构决定被正确实现？他们的决定最多是善意，除非跟进。

Finally, delegate some decision making to others who are experts in a problem domain. Many architects wrongly assume they have to make every architectural decision. Therefore, they position themselves as know-it-all experts. In reality, there’s no such thing as a universal technical genius. Architects have areas in which they are quite proficient, areas in which they are knowledgeable, and areas in which they are simply incompetent. Adept architects delegate decisions about domain problems in which they are not proficient.

最后，把一些决定委托给问题领域的专家。很多架构师错误地假设他们必须做每个架构决定。因此他们把自己定位为万事通专家。实际上没有万能技术天才这种东西。架构师有他们很精通的领域、有知识的领域、和根本不行的领域。娴熟的架构师把自己不精通的领域问题决定委托出去。

80. Don't Be Clever

作者：Eben Hewitt

General intelligence, resourcefulness, thoughtfulness, a breadth and depth of knowledge, and an affinity for precision are laudable qualities in anyone, and particularly prized in architects.

一般智力、机智、周到、知识的广度深度、以及对精确的亲和力在任何人身上都是值得称赞的品质，在架构师身上尤其珍贵。

Cleverness, however, carries a certain additional connotation. It implies an ability to quickly conceive of a solution that may get you out of a jam, but that ultimately rests on a gimmick, a shell game, or a switcharoo. We remember clever debaters from high school—always able to play semantics or work the logical fallacies to win the point.

然而，聪明带着某种额外含义。它暗示一种能快速想出把你从困境里救出来的方案的能力，但最终建立在花招、障眼法或调包上。我们记得高中聪明的辩手——总是能玩语义或用逻辑谬误赢点。

Clever software is expensive, hard to maintain, and brittle. Don’t be clever. Be as dumb as you possibly can and still create the appropriate design. The appropriate design will never be clever. If cleverness appears absolutely required, the problem is incorrectly framed; reset the problem. Reframe it until you can be dumb again. Work in rough chalk sketches; stay general. Let go of the flavor of the day. It takes a smart architect to be dumb.

聪明的软件昂贵、难维护、脆弱。别聪明。尽可能地笨，同时仍创建合适设计。合适的设计永远不会聪明。如果聪明看起来绝对需要，问题被错误框定了；重置问题。重新框定直到你能再笨。用粗糙粉笔草图工作；保持一般。放开当天的潮流。笨需要聪明的架构师。

It is our cleverness that allows us to trick software into working. Don’t be the attorney who gets your software off on a technicality. We are not Rube Goldberg. We are not MacGyver, ever ready to pull some complicated design out of our hats having been allowed only a paper clip, a firecracker, and a piece of chewing gum. Empty your head and approach the problem without your extensive knowledge of closures and generics and how to manipulate object graduation in the heap. Sometimes of course, such stuff is exactly what we need. But less often than we might think.

是我们的聪明让我们骗软件工作。别做那种靠技术细节把你软件捞出去的律师。我们不是 Rube Goldberg（那种搞极端复杂装置做简单事的）。我们不是 MacGyver——只给个回形针、鞭炮和口香糖就从帽子里抽出复杂设计。清空你的头，不带你对闭包和泛型以及怎么操纵堆里对象晋升的广博知识去面对问题。当然有时候这种东西正是我们需要的。但比我们以为的少。

More developers can implement and maintain dumb solutions. In dumb solutions, each component can do only one thing. They will take less time to create, and less time to change later. They inherit optimizations from the building blocks you’re using. They emerge from the page as a living process, and you can feel their elegance and simplicity. Clever designs will stay stubbornly rooted; their details are too embroiled in the overall picture. They crumble if you touch them.

更多开发能实现和维护笨方案。在笨方案里，每个组件只做一件事。创建它们花更少时间，以后改也花更少时间。它们从你用的构建块继承优化。它们从页面上作为活过程浮现，你能感到它们的优雅和简单。聪明的设计会顽固扎根；它们的细节缠在整体图里。你一碰就碎。
